title: Failed positive gate leaves the pipeline uninterpretable; 'null for the recipe' is not demonstrated
quote: training on reference solutions lowers pass@1 by 32.2 points, so the null
explanation:
The authors correctly refuse to generalise, but the title ('No Detectable Gain from Verifier-Filtered Self-Training of a 1.5B Model'), the opening framing (the 'cheapest and most widely used form of the loop') and the research question still address self-training. A drop of 30+ points from SFT on gold solutions (twice, at 5e-4 and in the corrected recipe at 1e-4) is not a mild failure to improve: it signals a defect in training/eval (truncation without EOS, loss on the prompt, sampling settings, fp16, evaluation cap) rather than a property of learning from data. Without a working positive control the experiment cannot discriminate 'verifier filtering does nothing' from 'any training here destroys the model', so even the null about the verifier is uninterpretable. The related-work analogy to Kim et al. (self-distillation on ground-truth cutting accuracy while shortening responses) is offered as an explanation but is not tested and does not explain a 32-point collapse. The contribution 'a null for the recipe' is thus a statement that the recipe is not a valid test bed.

Also (Positive gate failure is not diagnosed and may not certify the recipe): A 32-point collapse after one adapter trained on 300 examples (about 150 steps at batch size 2) at 1e-4 with completion-only loss and all-linear LoRA is far larger than ordinary SFT damage, and it is read as 'the recipe cannot help'. Two other readings are not excluded. (a) A pipeline or scoring fault: the model switches to the reference style ($-spans 60 to 1,577 of 1,600), and the verifier (including the stored-gold defect and unboxed answers) 

Also (Final-round gate failure (-32 points from 300 examples) is read as 'recipe cannot help', b): The gate is SFT of an already instruction-tuned Qwen2.5-1.5B on MATH-train reference solutions (very likely seen in its pretraining/post-training). Such data need not raise accuracy: they have a different format (the model moves to $-delimited prose, 60 to 1,577 of the generations), omit the prompted \boxed convention, and are not on-policy. Failing this gate shows that reference-solution SFT hurts under this format, not that no pipeline can help

Also (Gate failure is read as a recipe limitation without ruling out format/verifier or train-on): The central framing 'so the null concerns this recipe, not self-training in general' rests on train-on-gold lowering pass@1 by 32 points. But the paper shows the gold-trained model adopts the reference style ($-delimited spans in 1,577 of 1,600 generations), which the math-verify based scoring may not credit; in 4.4 the verifier-error bound covers only boxed answers (14% without \boxed uncovered), and for 4.6 no check at all of verifier error, bo

Also (A failed gate makes the pipeline, not only the recipe, uninterpretable; gate failure is no): A positive control is only informative if its failure can be attributed. Here training on 300 human MATH solutions drops pass@1 from 49.2 to 17.0, with $-delimited style adopted in 1,577 of 1,600 generations. Several explanations are not separated: (i) grading artifact - the same biased math-verify parses LaTeX only inside \boxed or $, gold storage is known to be defective, and 14% or more of generations in the older gold arms lack \boxed, so a s

Also (Conclusion draws a recipe-level null from a gate that failed, while Table 4 shows the loop): If the gate does not validate the recipe, the loop result (pass@1 -4.8 [-9.0, -0.6], the only 500-problem, corrected-recipe, single-seed comparison) cannot be read as a null for the recipe either: a recipe that damages the model by 30 points on trusted data may damage it on self-generated data by a smaller amount. The paper reads the loop as 'no gain and a possible small decline, as at 10^-5', but at 10^-5 no pass@1 interval excluded zero, wherea

Also (Headline 'no detectable gain' hides detected declines and an invalid test instrument): The title, abstract and conclusion frame the result as a null ('no detectable gain'). But the evidence is not a null: at 5e-4 every A/B run declines, with sample-accuracy intervals excluding zero in all four (Table 2), train-on-gold falls 18-32 points, the no-filter control falls, and the corrected-recipe loop loses 4.8 points of pass@1 with an interval excluding zero. Meanwhile the positive gate fails in both recipes, so the instrument cannot sh

title: Training recipe confounds (loss on prompt, truncated answers/EOS, q/v-only LoRA) plausibly drive the declines
quote:
loss over the whole chat sequence, prompt
included; fp16 on one Kaggle T4), with a training sequence limit of 512 tokens
that includes the prompt.
explanation:
Setup trains with loss on the prompt, LoRA only on q_proj/v_proj, 512-token limit including prompt, and 24-26% of the round-0 pool (62.4% in the no-filter control) truncated so that the final answer and EOS are cut. That means a quarter of positive examples teach the model to run on without a final answer, directly inducing the cap-hit rise later attributed to 'drift'. The headline learning rate 1e-5 is described as 'default of our training code and not tuned'; for LoRA r=16 this is one to two orders of magnitude below typical rates, so the main 5-round, k=8 Design I runs are near no-ops (the paper admits outputs change little), while the higher rates produce degradation likely from the truncation artifact. The fixes appear only in the late Sec. 4.6 corrected recipe, with one seed, 300 problems and 2 rounds. The reader is asked to accept a general-sounding null from a pipeline whose defects were found after most runs; the abstract and intro should say that the bulk of the evidence comes from the flawed recipe.

Also (Training truncation drops the answer and EOS in a quarter of the pool, so declines/nulls p): 24-26% of the round-0 pool (62.4% for no-filter) is cut in training and loses its final answer and end-of-sequence token, and the loss is taken over the prompt. Training the model on solutions with no EOS or answer plausibly drives the rise in cap-hits and the finished-accuracy decline, i.e. it is a pipeline defect confounded with the effect of self-training in every arm. title: Conditioning on the falling \boxed share removes the channel through which adaptation would show; 'no adaptation' is not identified
quote: fall matches the falling \boxed share among correct answers (91 → 76% and
explanation:
Algebraically r_all = r_boxed x boxed share (checked: 0.20x0.91=18.2, 0.207x0.76=15.7, 0.194x0.93=18.0, 0.198x0.78=15.4), so the overall fall is entirely the boxed-share fall; that arithmetic is right. But the paper elsewhere shows V's gold-storage defect removes about a fifth of V'-correct, boxed generations from the kept pool (440 vs 542), so the pool is systematically less boxed than the model's outputs, and V thereby rewards unboxing. A falling boxed share is therefore exactly what 'learning to write what V accepts' would produce, not a nuisance. Treating it as format drift that 'accounts for' the fall (Conclusion: 'once the falling \boxed share is accounted for') and the Discussion's 'imitation and drift would both produce' leave the audit unable to distinguish the hypothesis it was built to test. The boxed-share fall is not itself audited (no decomposition by affected vs unaffected problems, no share for the 10^-5 run).

Also ('No adaptation' conclusion is not identified: conditioning on boxed share removes the chan): The abstract, contribution 2 and conclusion say the fall in r_t is 'accounted for' by the falling \boxed share and therefore 'we find no adaptation'. But the paper itself states that a model adapting to the gold-storage defect 'would have to write these answers unboxed', i.e. adaptation would show up precisely as a lower boxed share. Explaining the r_t decline by the boxed share therefore cannot distinguish adaptation from drift/imitation (the pa

Also ('No adaptation' is stated more strongly than a power-less audit with same-direction estima): The audit has no positive control, 2-12 relevant training examples per round, and (for the only run with a pool of 9-12) a learning rate of 10^-5 where outputs barely change; the runs with a real update have pools of 2-5. So no run combines both pressure and capacity to adapt. The estimates on the cleanest subset (affected, parseable) are -5.5, -1.6 and -0.2, all in the adaptation direction, with intervals 10-26 points wide, and the overall falls

Also (Train-on-gold r_t rise is attributed to 'more boxed' outputs but boxed-only r_t rises almo): The same boxed-share identity is used to dismiss the fall in self-training runs. For train-on-gold, Table 5 shows boxed-only r_t rising +2.8 and +1.7 against overall +3.3 and +2.1, so only ~0.5 point of the rise is a boxed-share effect; most is a rise within boxed answers, which the boxed-share account cannot explain. Moreover 4.4 says train-on-gold adopts a $-delimited reference style (5% to 98%) and 14% of round-2 generations lack \boxed; no bo

title: Adaptation audit has almost no possible signal by construction
quote:
on the 54–62 problems where it ever ﬁres, it
rejects 94–98% of correct answers in every round, and 29–34 of these problems
have a gold the original veriﬁer cannot parse at all, so no answer form avoids
it there.
explanation: The audit asks whether the model learns to avoid the defect, yet by the paper's own numbers the defect is nearly unavoidable on the problems where it fires (94-98% rejection, and for 29-34 of 54-62 problems no answer form escapes it). Only 24-28 problems have an escaping form, and the affected examples removed from the pool number 2-12 per round out of hundreds. A fresh adapter per round with a handful of examples of selection pressure, at a learning rate that barely changes outputs, cannot be expected to produce measurable adaptation. The absence of a falling r_t is therefore predicted under the null and under the alternative, which the paper partly concedes ('no positive control') but still lists as a contribution and uses in the abstract ('we find no adaptation'). The 'carried over from RLVR' framing also overstates comparability: in RLVR the false negative directly zeroes the reward on every rollout, whereas here it removes at most a few examples. Relatedly, explaining the 1.5-2.6 point fall by a falling boxed share is asserted via a post hoc decomposition not specified in the Setup.

title: Detectable-effect rule and 2.2-point bound are post hoc, ignore seed variance and sit below the observed 3.2-point spread
quote:
a change would be
detected with 80% power at the 5% level only if it exceeded about 2.8 h/1.96
explanation:
The minimum detectable effect is computed from the half-widths h of the observed bootstrap intervals (post hoc power from the data), and those intervals, by the paper's own admission, cover only problem-sampling noise on a 150-problem exam and not training-seed variance. The one replicate pair differs by 3.2 points of sample accuracy, which is larger than the 2.2-point bound on gains claimed from the same measure, and larger than the 3.5 lower end of the detectable range. pass@1 is also a single draw at T=0.8 per problem, adding noise not in a problem-level bootstrap of 'first sample'. A 2.2-point exclusion bound is therefore not supportable as stated; with seed variance included the design likely detects only substantially larger effects, weakening the 'no gain of this size' conclusion. No multiplicity correction is applied while the paper reads 'patterns across runs' as evidence, which mixes correlated runs sharing partitions and seeds.

Also (Power rule is a post hoc MDE from observed intervals; no equivalence margin, so 'null' is ): The detectable effect is computed as 2.8 h/1.96 from half-widths h of the intervals actually observed, in runs whose estimates are already known (post hoc / observed power). More importantly it is a power statement, not an equivalence statement: a gain of exactly the MDE is still missed 20% of the time and smaller gains much more often, so 'a null means no gain of roughly that size' does not follow. No smallest effect of interest or equivalence (

Also (2.2-point sample-accuracy bound is a maximum of per-run upper limits, post hoc, and contra): The 2.2 figure is the largest upper limit among individual 95% intervals (e.g. A,1 and A,3 at 1e-4). It is selected from many runs, on a measure chosen after the runs, and without seed variance. The paper itself reports that its only same-configuration replicate pair ends 3.2 points of sample accuracy apart, which is larger than the bound and about as large as the claimed MDE (3.5-5.5). A bound tighter than the empirical run-to-run difference can

Also (2.2-point 'bound' is smaller than the observed seed-to-seed spread): The 2.2 figure is the largest upper limit among the sample-accuracy intervals in Table 2 (+2.2 for A at 1e-4, seeds 1 and 3). It is small because most point estimates are negative, not because the design is sensitive: Section 3.4 puts the detectable sample-accuracy effect at 3.5–5.5, and the only replicate pair differs by 3.2 points, larger than 2.2 (the two 5e-4 seeds of A differ by 8.3 vs 4.7). A bound that is tighter than the demonstrated run-

Also (Claimed power ('6-10 points') understates uncertainty and is uninformative for realistic e): The detectable-effect figures are derived from observed interval half-widths that, by the paper's own admission, omit training-seed variance (replicate pair ends 3.2 points apart; seed-to-seed differences of the same configuration exceed several of the reported effects). The 6-point figure for the final round comes from one seed, one rate, k=2, two rounds. The abstract states these as the design's power without that caveat. In addition, a minimum

Also (Headline power figure inconsistent: abstract says 6-10 points, body says about 10): Abstract reports a detectable effect of 6-10 points of pass@1, while the Introduction and Sec. 3.4 state 'about 10 points of pass@1' (and 8-10 for pass@k, 3.5-5.5 for sample accuracy). The 6 lower bound appears nowhere in the Setup derivation (which is based on Table 2 half-widths of the 150-problem exam). Since the paper's whole claim is 'null within the power of the design', the quoted power must be a single, derivable number; the abstract appe

Also (Detectable-effect ranges do not span the Table 2 half-widths of all MATH-500 arms): Applying 2.8h/1.96 (=1.43h) to Table 2 MATH-500 rows: sample accuracy gives 3.4 (A,0) to 5.7 (5e-4 / no-filter), but the train-on-gold rows (h=5.0 and 5.55, e.g. [-25.3,-14.2]) give 7.1 and 7.9. pass@k gives 8.6-9.6 for most rows but about 11.4-11.9 for gold (e.g. [-28.7,-12.7]) and 6.6 for Run C. The stated ranges therefore hold only if gold arms are excluded, which the text does not say. The abstract, intro, 5.1 and Conclusion headline figures 

Also (The A-vs-B contrast is an empirical null contrast showing the bootstrap intervals are too ): Runs A and B differ by 0-3 training examples (a de facto replicate), yet B minus A is +5.3 at seed 1 and -7.3 with an interval excluding zero at seed 2. This is a direct calibration check of the interval procedure: for a contrast with a true effect of about zero, the problem-level bootstrap produced a 'significant' result, so it omits a variance source (training/trajectory noise) that is at least as large as the sampling noise. title: Same-seed arms, rate dose-response and cross-arm dose/k/rounds confounds make comparisons uninterpretable
quote: accuracy intervals exclude zero in all four A/B runs
explanation:
Within a seed, A, B, no-filter, train-on-gold and the three learning rates all share the same 150-problem exam and the same round-0 generations (round 0 is identical, 33.3 / 50.0 for every seed-1 row). All 'declines' are therefore measured against one stochastic baseline draw per seed: if round 0 happened to be a high draw, every arm declines together (regression to the mean) and the declines are perfectly correlated, not replicated. Effectively the 5e-4 evidence is two exam/baseline draws, not four runs, and the paper does acknowledge A/B pairs are 'closer to two replicates' but then still tallies 'five of six' and 'every run declines' as pattern evidence and says it rests conclusions on patterns across runs. With no multiplicity correction and ~17 runs x 4 metrics, a handful of excluded-zero intervals are also expected by chance. Conversely the main null on gains is conservative with respect to multiplicity, but the decline claims at the highest rate are not. The effective sample size should be counted per (seed, partition), and the baseline should be re-measured with several generation seeds.

Also (Rate dose-response is read from two seeds that disagree): The claim that the decline 'may grow with the rate' rests on seed 1 alone; seed 2 is 'almost flat' (3.7, 3.8, 4.7). The differences between rates (1.5 vs 3.5) are smaller than the 3.2-point gap between a replicate pair and than the A-vs-B pass@1 swing of 12.6 points at 5e-4. Rates also differ in effective steps and truncation. With intervals that omit training-seed variance, no rate effect is identifiable; even the 8.3 vs 4.7 difference at 5e-4 i

Also (The tested manipulations range from near no-op to damaging; the 'any learning rate' null i): At 1e-5 the paper itself says outputs barely changed (weak evidence the adapter did little), so a null there is the expected result for an almost identity update and says nothing about self-training. Rates that do move the model (5e-4) all lower accuracy, and the gate shows that even gold data lowers it by 18-32 points. No rate sits in a regime where training both changes the model and is plausibly beneficial. 'No detectable gain at any learning 

Also (Cross-arm dose, k, rounds and metric confounds make the controls and the rate comparisons ): Optimizer steps equal half the kept-pool size, and pool size depends on the model's own accuracy and the verifier's acceptance, so dose is an outcome of the intervention, not a controlled variable, and it differs between A, B, no-filter (1400 examples, 3-4x steps) and gold (350). The 1e-5 and higher-rate runs differ in k (8 vs 4), rounds (5 vs 3) and metric (pass@8 vs pass@4), so the abstract's 'four learning rates' is not a clean rate sweep, and

Also (Claims of generality beyond a single model family, single verifier and few seeds): The scope is Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct only (0.5B only in the pooled design), one verifier, LoRA on q/v, one epoch, a 150-problem exam, and learning rates from 1e-5 to 5e-4 with different k and round counts between rates (the paper says only the comparison among 1e-4, 2e-4, 5e-4 isolates the rate). Only the 1e-4 rate has three seeds; GSM8K appears only at 1e-5 per the Setup. The abstract states 'four learning rates on MATH-500 and two on GSM8K' but S

title: Final round is a single adapter, single seed, post hoc and exploratory; it cannot speak to the iterated loop
quote: It is one seed at 10−4 with k = 2 and two rounds.
explanation:
'Two rounds' here means round 0 plus one adapter (the table reports untrained to round 1). No second self-training iteration, and so no compounding, is tested. The Conclusion and Section 5.1 use this result to answer whether 'generate–verify–select–train iterations' help, and the Limitations list 'a restart-from-base design that leaves compounding little room'. With one seed, one adapter and a failed gate, the new round adds little to the multi-round question; the extra power (500 problems) addresses only problem sampling, not seed variance, so the 'detectable effect about 6' is a lower bound on what a single seed can resolve.

Also (The 'loop' in the final round is a single adapter from base: nothing about iteration, comp): By the paper's own definitions (restart from base, round 0 is the untrained model, Table 4 reports 'untrained model to round 1'), two rounds means exactly one adapter trained once on the round-0 pool of 298 examples (about 150 steps). That is one-shot rejection-sampling fine-tuning, not a generate-verify-select-train loop. The paper concedes that restart-from-base gives compounding little room, so what it can say about 'several GVT rounds' (resea

Also (Final round is post hoc and data-dependent but not listed among the post hoc choices; the ): The Introduction enumerates what was chosen after seeing runs (higher learning rates, controls, round count, k, primary measure, re-scoring) but does not list the final round (new recipe, k=2, 2 rounds, 300-problem pool, one seed, lr 1e-4), which was designed after earlier arms failed and is described as using 'changes a reviewer asked for'. The Introduction's summary of the answer ('no improvement ... at any learning rate we tried') also does no

Also (Repeated reuse of the same 500 problems for design decisions makes the exam adaptive; the ): All decisions (higher rates, k, rounds, sample accuracy as primary, which controls to run, which recipe fixes) were taken after seeing results on partitions of the same 500 MATH-500 problems, and the final round then uses all 500 as the exam. Seeds 1-3 draw overlapping 150-problem exams from this pool, so the exams are not independent. The final round's recipe was chosen after reviewer criticism of earlier exam results and is evaluated on those s

Also (Headline final-round result singles out the one interval that excludes zero, one seed, thr): In Table 4 the loop's pass@2 interval ([-6.8,+0.6]) and sample-accuracy interval ([-5.8, 0.0]) both touch or include zero; only pass@1, computed from the first of just two samples per problem (the noisiest metric), excludes zero, with an upper limit of -0.6. The abstract reports only this one. With one seed, no training-seed variance (shown elsewhere to be at least as large as the sampling noise), and three correlated measures, the evidence for a

Also (Final-round decline rests on first-draw pass@1; sample accuracy and 10^-5 comparison do no): With k = 2, sample accuracy is the mean of the two draws, so a sample-accuracy change of −2.9 and a pass@1 change of −4.8 imply the second draw fell only about 1.0 point. The pass@1 headline is therefore partly a feature of which draw is called 'first', and it is the more extreme of two estimates of the same quantity. The pass@1 interval (−9.0, −0.6) only just excludes zero; the sample-accuracy interval (−5.8, 0.0) touches it; pass@2 includes zer

title: Earlier 5e-4 gate (-30.5) is unsourced and the gate was tried only at high rates
quote: An earlier gate at 5 × 10−4 with the same recipe also failed (−30.5 points
explanation:
The −30.5 pass@1 change appears in no table and has no interval or seed, and its exam partition is not stated. The train-on-gold arms in Table 3 (old recipe, 150-problem exams) fall −18.0 and −21.3 pass@1 at 5e-4, so −30.5 must come from a different run, yet it is called the 'same recipe' as the corrected one, which is described as one seed at 1e-4. Section 5.1 and Section 6 then say the gate failed 'twice', while Table 3 already has two failed gold arms. The count of failed gates, and which recipe each used, is inconsistent and not traceable.

Also (Earlier 5e-4 gate result (-30.5) is cited as 'same recipe' but is not reported anywhere in): The only train-on-gold results at 5e-4 in Tables 2-3 are under the original recipe (q/v LoRA, prompt loss, 512 cap) and give pass@1 changes of -18.0 / -21.3 at R2 (-15.3 and -22.6 at R1), not -30.5. So the -30.5 must come from an unreported run with the corrected recipe; its seed, k, rounds and interval are not given, and 5.1/6 then count the gate as having 'failed twice'. 'Same recipe' is also ambiguous between the original and the corrected rec

Also (Gate tried only at high rates, an undocumented second gate run, and a stopping rule applie): The text says the earlier 5e-4 gate used 'the same recipe', yet the corrected recipe (completion-only loss, all-linear, 1,024 cap, normalised gold, MATH-train pool) is introduced only in 4.6, and the gold arms reported in Tables 2-3 at 5e-4 used the old recipe and fell -18.0 / -21.3, not -30.5. So either a further run exists that appears in no table, or the sentence is wrong. Either way, the number of recipe variants and gates attempted before re

title: Cap-share decomposition is undefined, unstable across seeds and the cap-hit proxy is not the generation-time criterion
quote: (and −2 and 5% in the replicate and the 1,024-limit run) and 52–72% at seed 2
explanation:
Using Table 1 for A at 5e-4, seed 2: cap-hit rises from 43.1% to 51.2% (+8.1) while sample accuracy falls 30.8 to 26.2. If capped generations are essentially never correct, finished accuracy goes from about 54% to about 54%, so the cap share would explain nearly all the decline (over 90%), not 52–72%. Yet the matched finished accuracy in Table 2 is −5.5 for the same run, which would imply a large finished-accuracy loss as well. The two measures cannot both hold under an additive split, and the decomposition formula is not in the main text (only 'Table ??'). At seed 1 the same arithmetic gives about 22%, in line with 12–30%, so the inconsistency is specific to seed 2. The conclusion that the balance 'differs by partition' and that the effect is clear 'at one of two seeds' depends on this decomposition.

Also (Cap-share decomposition is undefined in the main text and its shares do not reconcile with): Recomputing the standard decomposition (finished share x finished accuracy) from Tables 1-2 at 5e-4: at seed 1, finished share about 0.57, matched finished loss 9.1 gives about -5.2, cap-share change -3 pts times baseline finished accuracy about 0.59 gives about -1.9, sum about -7 versus an observed sample-accuracy fall of 8.3. At seed 2, finished loss 5.5 gives about -3.1 and the 8-point cap rise gives about -4.3 (sum about -7.4) versus an obser

Also (Conclusion emphasises finished-accuracy loss although the decomposition says cap share dom): Section 4.5/5.3 report that the cap share explains 52-72% of the decline at seed 2 and only 12-30% at seed 1, and the matched finished-accuracy interval for A at seed 2 is [-11.7, 0.1] (includes zero; the 'five of six' count rests on that). The Conclusion states as the primary finding that accuracy on finished solutions falls, with cap-hits only 'clearly at one of two seeds'. The two seeds disagree on the mechanism, with different exam partitions

Also (Cap-decomposition contribution stated more strongly than the descriptive, partition-depend): Contribution 3 presents the decomposition as a result: finished generations lose 5.5-10.6 points. But (a) the range pools A, B and the no-filter control (so not purely verifier-filtered self-training); (b) the interval for A seed 2 includes zero (-5.5 [-11.7, 0.1]) and Sec 4.5 admits only 'five of six' exclude zero, and the six include near-replicate A/B pairs; (c) the matched measure conditions on which problems finish after training and uses ro

Also (Cap-hit proxy (>= 508 re-tokenised tokens) is not the generation-time criterion and cannot): Section 3.4 states that token counts at generation time were not saved. Re-tokenised length of decoded text can differ from the generated token count (special tokens, merges across the decode boundary), and the 4-token margin is not justified; generations that finish between 508 and 512 tokens are classified as unfinished, and the paper's own earlier character proxy is said to have been misleading. Every cap-share and 'finished accuracy' number i

title: 'No run/arm improves' and 'no detectable gain' hide detected declines and positive point estimates
quote: No arm improves on round 0, and the gate on
explanation: Absolute statements 'no run improves pass@1 or pass@k', 'No arm improves' (contributions, 5.1, Limitations, Conclusion) are literally contradicted by the paper's own tables: A seed 1 at 1e-4 has +0.7 pass@1, A seed 3 +1.3 pass@k, A seed 1 at 1e-5 +0.0, and in Table 3 the no-filter arm at seed 2 rises from 31.3 to 34.7 pass@1 at round 1 and the 'largest rise' is quoted in 5.1. Section 5.1 correctly says no rise has an interval excluding zero; the conclusion and limitations drop that qualifier, and the 'no positive reference' argument (null is about the recipe) relies on this stronger version. Statistically insignificant positive changes should not be described as no improvement.

title: 'Removing the filter made no difference of consistent sign' is contradicted by the tables
quote: Patching a rare veriﬁer defect and removing the ﬁlter made no diﬀerence of consistent
explanation:
Against Run A at the same seed, no-filter is worse on pass@k (-9.3 vs -7.3; -12.0 vs -6.7), on pass@4 at R2 (-2.0 and -5.3, stated in 4.4), on matched finished accuracy (-10.6 vs -9.1; -6.6 vs -5.5), equal or worse on sample accuracy (-8.2 vs -8.3; -10.2 vs -4.7); only pass@1 at seed 1 favours no-filter (-6.0 vs -10.0). That is a consistent sign on most measures, though confounded by dose (3-4x steps) and within noise. The paper's own 4.4 text concedes it is 'lower on pass@4 at both seeds'. 5.2 and the Conclusion should say 'no difference that can be separated from dose and noise' rather than 'no consistent sign', or at least not group it with the patch (where signs flip).

Also (Conclusion says removing the filter made 'no difference of consistent sign' while the data): The conclusion (and 5.2: 'made no consistent diﬀerence') says patching and removing the filter made no difference of consistent sign. For the no-filter control, however, pass@4 is lower than the filtered loop at both seeds (-2.0 and -5.3 at round 2, as 4.4 itself says), pass@k changes in Table 2 are more negative at both seeds (-9.3, -12.0 vs -7.3, -6.7), and the matched finished accuracy is worse at both seeds (-10.6 vs -9.1; -6.6 vs -5.5). The

title: Gold-storage defect 'ran unvaried' is unclear now that Sec 4.6 uses normalised gold
quote: gold-storage defect was measured afterwards and ran unvaried through every
explanation: Section 4.6 states that the corrected-recipe round uses 'normalised gold answers'. If this removes the bare-gold storage defect (the paper never says whether it does, nor reports r_t or the V/V' gap for that round), then the defect was varied in the final round and the statements 'ran unvaried through every experiment' (Conclusion, Limitations), 'was never varied' (5.2) and 'a dose-matched control for the gold-storage defect ... come first' are inconsistent with the paper's own design; if it does not, the text should say so. Either way the single run that is the paper's only 500-problem, corrected-recipe evidence is not tied to the audit or the defect analysis, and the headline claims are not updated to say which experiment is clean of the defect.

title: Final-round pass@k detectable effect is misquoted (4 vs about 5.3)
quote: only about 10 points of pass@1 and 8–10 of pass@k (6 and 4 in the ﬁnal round)
explanation:
Section 4.6 gives pass@2 for the loop as −3.0 [−6.8, +0.6], half-width 3.8. By the paper's own rule (2.8h/1.96) the detectable pass@2 effect is about 5.4 points, not 4. Pass@1 (h about 4.2 gives 6.0) is right, and 4 would fit sample accuracy (−2.9 [−5.8, 0.0], h 2.9 gives about 4.1), but the sentence pairs it with pass@k, and the 150-problem contrast (8–10 for pass@k) is a pass@k contrast. Section 6 and Section 7 repeat only the pass@1 value (6), so only 5.1 is wrong. All of these also omit seed variance, so the 6-point figure is optimistic for a single seed.

Also (Detectable-effect numbers for the final round: pass@k bound of 4 does not follow from Tabl): The paper's rule is detectable effect = 2.8h/1.96 with h the interval half-width. In Table 4 the loop's pass@1 half-width is 4.2 (gives 6.0, matches the text) but the pass@2 interval [-6.8, +0.6] has half-width 3.7, giving about 5.3, not 4; the figure 4 matches the sample-accuracy half-width (2.9, giving about 4.1). So '6 and 4' pairs pass@1 and pass@k in the sentence but the second number is the sample-accuracy figure. The same pairing appears i

Also (Final-round power figure for pass@k ('4') does not follow from the reported interval): Using the paper's own formula (2.8h/1.96) with the final-round pass@2 interval [-6.8, +0.6] (half-width about 3.7) gives roughly 5.3 points, not 4; the value of about 4 matches sample accuracy (half-width about 2.9 gives about 4.1), not pass@k. The Conclusion lists only 6 for the final round, and the abstract '6-10' omits pass@k. So the parenthetical mismatches the measure it is attached to and overstates the final round's pass@k resolution.

Also (Final-round pass@k detectable effect stated as 4, but Table 4 half-width gives about 5.3): Section 4.6 derives the 500-problem detectable effect as 2.8h/1.96 with h about 4 for pass@1 (interval [-9.0,-0.6], h=4.2, giving 6.0, which matches). The same formula applied to pass@2 in Table 4 ([-6.8,+0.6], h=3.7) gives about 5.3, not 4. The sample-accuracy interval ([-5.8,0.0], h=2.9) gives about 4.1, so the '4' appears to come from the wrong measure, or is mislabeled as pass@k. Also (Final-round detectable effect for pass@k is misquoted (4 vs about 5.3 implied by Table 4)): The paper's rule is MDE = 2.8 h/1.96. In Table 4 the loop's pass@2 interval is [-6.8, +0.6], so h = 3.7 and MDE about 5.3, and the gold arm's pass@2 gives h = 4.7 (MDE about 6.7). Pass@1 gives h about 4.2 and MDE about 6.0, which matches the stated 6. title: Verifier false-negative evidence is small, other-model-sourced and not reconciled with Huang et al. or the 15.5-18.3% figure
quote:
the false-negative rate is 7.8% (10 of 128; Wilson interval
4.3–13.8%) on MATH-500 and 0% on GSM8K.
explanation:
The rate is estimated on public solutions of Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (not the 1.5B policy, with different answer styles) for 200 problems, where 'correct' is defined by the authors' own scripted normalised comparison, whose own error rate is unreported; only 128 solutions qualify. The GSM8K 0% has no denominator. Then the same section reports that the gold-storage defect rejects 15.5-18.3% of V'-accepted generations of the loop itself, roughly double the 7.8%; the text says 8 of the 10 failures are 'probably largely' the storage defect, but never reconciles why the real policy suffers twice the rate, nor whether the 7.8% was measured with the faulty bare gold. Because the headline motivation (verifier rejects correct answers) rests on these numbers, the measurement pipeline and the relation between the two estimates need specifying. The statement that the audit gives 'no false-positive rate' also leaves the more consequential verifier error (false accepts in the pool, which Egashira et al. find harmful) completely unmeasured while the paper frames the study around what the verifier accepts.

Also (Huang et al. math-verify recall not reconciled with own measurements): Related Work cites 0.95 recall for math-verify on MATH, but Sec 3.2 measures a 7.8% false-negative rate (recall about 0.92) on MATH-500 and a gold-storage defect rejecting about one in six accepted generations. The discrepancy is not discussed; either the pipeline defect, not the verifier, explains it (so the cited verifier-error literature is not directly relevant to the paper's headline 'verifier' framing) or the cited benchmark differs. title: Qwen2.5 contamination on MATH/GSM8K gets three words in Limitations
quote: possible test-set contamination
explanation: Qwen2.5-Instruct is trained on large math corpora that include the MATH and GSM8K training distributions and plausibly test-adjacent data, and the exam consists of the public first 500 GSM8K test and the MATH-500 problems. If the exam answers are partly memorised, accuracy is dominated by recall that fine-tuning on self-generated samples has no room to improve (a ceiling-type null) and the effect of fine-tuning on human MATH-train solutions that the model has already seen in pre/post-training would be expected to be neutral or harmful, which undermines the gate's interpretation. Contamination also makes the 'amplify not expand' reading ambiguous. No decontamination check (n-gram overlap, perturbed-problem accuracy, performance on a post-cutoff set) or sensitivity analysis is reported, and the Limitations mention does not state which direction it biases the main conclusion. A fresh held-out set or perturbed variants would resolve this.

title: Defect rejection 94-98% vs Table 5, and 440->542 implying 18.8%, are not reconciled
quote: it rejects 94–98% of correct answers in every round
explanation:
Section 3.2 and 5.3 say that on the 54-62 problems where the defect fires, 94-98% of correct answers are rejected in every round. Table 5's 'affected, parseable' row, which is the same r_t quantity restricted to 24-28 of those problems, is 92.8, 95.1, 92.3 at round 0 and falls to 87.2 in the last round for A at 5e-4 seed 1. The remaining 29-34 unparseable-gold problems would have to be at roughly 100% to pull the union back up to 94%. This is arithmetically possible but never shown, and 87.2 is the very change (-5.5) the text calls noise, so a reader cannot reconcile 'in every round 94-98%' with the table.

Also (Round-0 pool enlargement (440 to 542) implies an 18.8% reject share, above the stated 15.5): If 542 examples are accepted by V′ and 440 by V, V rejects 102/542 = 18.8% of V′-accepted solutions, which is outside the stated 15.5–18.3% range (the Table 5 round-0 values are 18.0–18.3). Either the pool figures come from a different set (e.g. different seed or run) than the rates, or the range is wrong; the text does not say. The 'about a fifth to a quarter' dose and the claim that the defect would change a larger share of the pool than the 0–

title: Table 2 mixes run-log and recomputed values; patch-control explanation is unclear
quote: seed 1 (recomputed from the saved generations; Table 2 lists values from the
explanation:
Section 4.3 gives B minus A at seed 1 as +0.0 [−2.7, +2.7] from recomputed generations, whereas Table 2 lists B,1 at −4.0 and A,1 at −3.3, whose difference is −0.7. Intervals in Table 2 are said to be bootstrapped from saved generations, but the point estimates are from run logs. Six round values differ by one problem. Not consequential for conclusions, but the headline table is not the same data as the text's recomputation, and the interval centres may not match the generation-based estimates.

Also (Patch-control seed-0 difference and the explanation of which value comes from run logs are): Table 2 pass@1 at 1e-5 gives B,0 -3.3 minus A,0 -2.7 = -0.6 (-0.67 unrounded), and B,1 -4.0 minus A,1 -3.3 = -0.7. The following parenthetical says Table 2 'lists values from the run logs that differ by one problem, giving -0.7', which refers to seed 1 (recomputed +0.0 versus table -0.7) but reads as if it applied to the seed-0 figure just quoted. Thus the text's seed-1 value (+0.0) contradicts Table 2 (-0.7) for the headline control comparison,

title: Audit is listed as a contribution though admitted non-novel and unvalidated; novelty claims too broad
quote: A post hoc per-round false-reject audit of one
explanation:
Contribution 2 claims the audit as a contribution, yet Related Work states the measurement is the per-step tracking of Egashira et al. and TinyV, Sec 5.3 says the four checks are 'not tested methods', and the audit has no positive control and low power. The only novelty is transplanting a known measurement to offline SFT, with a null result that cannot distinguish adaptation from no adaptation. An unvalidated protocol (checks iii-iv are generic advice: dose-matching, check the dose of a control) does not justify a contribution; it should be moved to discussion or validated with a synthetic positive control (e.g. injected defect with known adaptation pressure).

Also (Self-contradictory novelty statement for the audit): Related Work says the per-round measurement is not new, while the Introduction contributions list and Conclusion present it as the paper's second contribution ('carried over from RLVR'). The remaining distinct piece (a gold-storage defect of the authors' own pipeline) is a pipeline bug, not a property of verifiers in general, which weakens the generality of the claimed audit.

Also (Proposed protocol offered without validation): Sec 5.3 recommends four checks as a protocol and the Conclusion says the audit 'asks part of that question whether accuracy rises or falls', yet the authors concede no positive control exists, so the audit's sensitivity is unknown. The recommendation to apply it to public RLVR checkpoints extrapolates from a null that the authors say cannot rule adaptation out; this is a hypothesis, not a finding.

Also (Novelty claim in Related Work is stronger than the cited literature supports and is incons): This sweeping statement about STaR, ReST, ReST-EM and RFT is unverified, and the same section immediately cites TinyV and From Accuracy to Robustness, which do study how rule-based verifiers' errors depend on answer format. Later the section says the per-round false-reject measurement 'is not new either' and that the authors 'do not claim this combination as the contribution', yet the Introduction's contributions list still presents the audit as 

Also (Overbroad statement about prior self-training work): The claim that STaR, ReST, ReST-EM and RFT do not measure how filter errors depend on answer form is stated as a universal negative about four works with no supporting search described; the authors' own later sentence ('We found no multi-round study...') is hedged but this one is not. Also later cites TinyV and Huang et al. on verifier errors that relate to the same dependence.

title: Closest work (Xu et al.) overlaps the decomposition and its lessons are not applied
quote: draw and sampling, not training-seed variance; several conditions have one seed,
explanation:
Related Work says Xu et al. [15], the closest study, found that uncontrolled training-seed variance (among seven failures) can invert a finding, and cites this as motivation. The paper then reports single-seed conditions with intervals that omit training-seed variance, including the final round (one seed) that carries the strongest claim (-4.8 points, interval excluding zero). Standards demanded by the cited work are not met, and the 'difference' from [15] is mostly scale and verifier type.

Also (Distinctness from Xu et al. is thin; decomposition overlaps their finding): Related Work credits Xu et al. [15] with identifying a fixed token cap under style drift as a measurement failure and says this is why finished accuracy is separated from termination. Contribution 3 then lists the finished-accuracy/cap-share decomposition as new. It is an application of an already-reported failure mode, and Sec 5.3 itself calls the split 'descriptive'. The novelty claim should be scoped accordingly.

title: Research question and title promise a verifier answer the data leave open
quote:
In hindsight the rule is one-sided: it can only ﬁre when accuracy rises (Sec-
tion 5.1).
explanation:
The title asks 'Mathematics or the Verifier?' and the intro poses a two-branch question, but the only pre-specified decision rule cannot fire unless accuracy rises, which never happens; so the 'verifier-style' branch is not tested by any pre-set criterion and the intro admits 'the pre-set rule is silent'. The substitute is a post hoc audit of the gold-storage defect, which Sec. 3.2 describes as a property of 'our pipeline' (the gold stored without delimiter), not of math-verify's behaviour on answer forms. Section 3.2 is nevertheless titled 'The Verifier and Its Directional Bias', and the abstract/related work frame it as verifier bias. The paper should state clearly that the verifier-adaptation question is unaddressed, and that the studied defect is an implementation error of the authors, whose fix (V') they had available but did not use in the loop.

Also (Title/framing promises a verifier question the data leave open, with a pipeline bug as the): The title and abstract frame the study around 'Mathematics or the Verifier?', and cite the verifier-bias literature, but the paper concludes the verifier question is open and the only substantive 'verifier' defect examined is the authors' own gold-storage choice, which is an implementation error rather than math-verify behaviour. The relation to Egashira (systematic false negatives behave like noise) and TinyV (verifier error) is thus weaker than

title: Cited findings (Wang, Kim, TinyV) are characterised loosely; many 2026 preprints cannot be verified
quote: report only 8.6 of their 37.6 points as lying beyond it, but the studies mostly do
explanation:
The Introduction says the one-example gain has 'only 8.6 points beyond format correction'; Related Work says 'the studies mostly do not ask what the rest consists of' immediately after crediting Wang et al. and Shao et al. with asking exactly that. The 8.6/37.6 figures are not verifiable from the text (37.6 is the difference of 73.6 and 36.0) and the attribution of this decomposition to Wang et al. should be checked against the source. Also the claim that Wang separates format correction is used to motivate a verifier-adaptation question that Wang does not address.

Also (Kim et al. comparison is speculative and ill-matched): Kim et al. study self-distillation conditioned on ground truth, where degradation is tied to suppressed uncertainty expression/shortened reasoning. The paper's train-on-gold arm loses 32 points (and 30.5 at an earlier gate) which, given the failed gate and the authors' own concern about recipe (loss over prompt, truncation), is more plausibly a pipeline artefact. Claiming a 'similar surface signature' without showing response-length statistics bo

Also (TinyV described as tracking false negatives across steps - unverifiable and doubtful): TinyV is principally a verifier-augmentation method (LLM fallback to reduce false negatives); the text attributes to it per-step tracking of false-negative share and uses [4,16] jointly as the source of the audit. This characterisation is not supported in the paper by any figure or quote and, if inaccurate, undercuts the claim that the audit is 'carried over' from two sources. Also, 'Xu et al.' is ambiguous because refs 15 (Xu, C.) and 16 (Xu, Z.

Also (Heavy reliance on single-author or very recent preprints, cannot be verified): Several load-bearing references are 2026 arXiv preprints (Egashira 2605.02909, Qiao 2606.13732, Strozzi 2606.07856, Xu 2608.20290, Kim 2603.24472), including a single-author one whose phrase 'amplifies but does not compound' is quoted to support the narrative and an Xu et al. paper described as 'closest to ours' and used as the main standard. title: Reproducibility gaps: unsaved logs/outputs, unspecified seeds and splits
quote:
token counts at generation time, Design P’s training logs and the
1,536-token re-scoring outputs were not saved.
explanation: Several quantities used in results (cap-hit shares are computed by re-tokenising decoded text rather than from generation-time counts; the Design P collapse that motivates the study; the 1,536-token re-scoring that is never introduced in the Setup) rely on artefacts that were not kept, so a reader cannot recompute them. The Setup also does not give the seeds, the exam/selection split procedure beyond '30%', the generation stop conditions, the adapter initialisation, or how many optimizer steps each run used, and the exam is evaluated by single-sample pass@1 at temperature 0.8 with repetition penalty 1.1, a setting which depresses and adds variance to accuracy relative to greedy evaluation. The mention of the pre-registered 'four measures' is not backed by a dated record. For a negative result whose value depends on the exact protocol, these omissions matter.

title: Style-count denominator (1,600) does not match 500 problems x k=2
quote: the model adopts the reference style ($-delimited spans in 60 of
explanation:
The exam is 500 problems at k = 2 (1,000 generations), and the 300-problem pool adds 600 more, so 1,600 seems to be exam plus selection generations at round 0. This is not stated, and it differs from the exam-only denominators used for the earlier $-span share (5% to 98%) and for the Table 4 metrics. A reader cannot tell whether 3.8% and 98.6% refer to the evaluated generations.

Also (Denominator of the style count does not match 500 problems x k = 2): The final round has 500 exam problems and k = 2, i.e. 1,000 exam generations (and 600 pool generations if the 300 pool problems are also sampled, 1,600 in total only if both are counted). The text does not say which population the 1,600 refers to, and the style counts at round 1 include generations from a model that was trained on exactly these pool problems; mixing the exam and training partitions would inflate the adoption figure relative to he

Also (Generation count in final-round style check (1,600) does not match 500 problems x k=2): Section 4.6 and Table 4 define the exam as 500 problems with k=2, i.e. 1,000 exam generations per round. A count of 1,577 dollar-delimited spans out of only 1,000 would exceed 100%, and 1,600 is never explained (it matches 600 pool generations plus 1,000 exam generations, but the text does not say the count pools them).
